expected_segments: Reading a road means combining instructions, movement, visibility and uncertainty. A sign tells you something important; it rarely tells you everything needed for the next decision.

In this chapter M03-L01 · Recognise what a sign asks M03-L02 · Combine the instructions M03-L03 · Find your way without rushing M03-L04 · Leave room to respond M03-R · Review and self-assessment Answers and review guidance Sources and references This material is a learning aid to help you understand Swedish driving theory. It is not an official source and cannot replace official information from Trafikverket and Transportstyrelsen. Always consult their current guidance and the applicable rules.
Your goal: Classify the main sign families and describe the decision each one prompts.

Start with purpose, then read the specific symbol and any supplementary panel. The official catalogue groups signs by function. Do not rely on colour alone: similar shapes can communicate different duties, and some important signs have distinctive shapes. Transportstyrelsen: sign catalogue
Five sign families Separate examples, not a roadside assembly. Read each caption as well as the shape and colour.
Children often cross or remain near this stretch. The sign supplies a warning, not a numerical speed limit. Two children inside a warning triangle.
Children ahead. Two children inside a warning triangle.
Yield to vehicles on the crossing road or route. With a distance or stop-ahead panel, this can instead be advance information. Inverted triangular give-way sign.
Give way. Inverted triangular give-way sign.
Continue the learning
Do not exceed the displayed speed in km/h. A junction alone does not necessarily end the limit, and conditions may require a lower speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 30: maximum 30 km/h.
Maximum speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 30: maximum 30 km/h.
Travel only in a direction shown by the arrow or arrows. Arrow points left.
Mandatory direction. Arrow points left.
A built-up area begins. Establish the applicable speed limit and other rules; a separate sign may prescribe a different limit. Black settlement skyline on white.
Built-up area. Black settlement skyline on white.
Continue the learning
Family
What to establish
A useful driving question
A — warning
The nature of a hazard ahead
What might be hidden, and how much space do I need?
B — priority
A duty or relationship at a conflict point
Must I yield or stop, and to whom?
C — prohibition/restriction
What movement, vehicle or limit is restricted
Does this apply to my vehicle and journey?
D — mandatory instruction
The required route, side or permitted traffic
Which path must I take?
E — instruction
A road or area with a particular meaning or regime
Which rules begin or end here?

These are learning questions, not substitutes for the individual sign descriptions. A warning of children, for example, does not assign a new numerical speed by itself; your speed must still allow safe control and a response to foreseeable hazards. A posted maximum speed is a ceiling, not a demand to maintain that speed. Road Signs Regulation, chapter 2 · Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§14–15

Requirements. B1 means yield to vehicles on the crossing road or route. Make that intention clear early and proceed only without danger or obstruction. B2 requires a stop before entering the crossing road or track area. Stop at the stop line; without one, stop immediately before the signal or before entering the crossing road or track area, as applicable. A rolling pause does not meet a stop duty. Road Signs Regulation, B1–B2 · Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§5 and 19
Yield and stop Signs and markings are labelled teaching counterparts. These examples do not establish their position in a particular road scene.
Yield to vehicles on the crossing road or route. With a distance or stop-ahead panel, this can instead be advance information. Inverted triangular give-way sign.
Give way. Inverted triangular give-way sign.
Make a complete stop before entering the crossing road, route or track area. Use the stop line; without one, apply the prescribed stopping position. Red octagon bearing STOP.
Stop. Red octagon bearing STOP.
This identifies where to stop when a sign or signal requires it. The line alone does not create a universal stop duty. Wide transverse white stop line.
Stop line. Wide transverse white stop line.
Continue the learning
This identifies the line drivers should not pass while yielding. Row of white give-way triangles.
Give-way line. Row of white give-way triangles.
Prepare for a yielding or stopping duty further ahead in your direction. White inverted triangle painted on the road.
Give way or stop ahead marking. White inverted triangle painted on the road.
Apply the learning
A narrow rural bridge with an oncoming van. The scene shows the approach; the separate official examples explain warnings and priority. Not to scale.

Worked decision. You see a warning sign for a narrow section. You reduce speed and look for oncoming traffic before reaching it. You then read any priority instruction at the narrow point. The warning alone did not decide who should pass first.
Narrow roads: warning and priority Compare the three narrowing shapes. B6 and B7 show opposing viewpoints, never simultaneous instructions to one approach.
Expect less road width ahead. The warning does not by itself decide priority over oncoming traffic. The road narrows on both sides.
Road narrows. The road narrows on both sides.
Expect less road width ahead. The warning does not by itself decide priority over oncoming traffic. The road narrows from the right.
Road narrows. The road narrows from the right.
Expect less road width ahead. The warning does not by itself decide priority over oncoming traffic. The road narrows from the left.
Road narrows. The road narrows from the left.
Continue the learning
Yield to oncoming vehicles at the restricted section. Upward red arrow beside a downward black arrow.
Give way to oncoming traffic. Upward red arrow beside a downward black arrow.
Oncoming vehicles have the yielding duty. Do not force passage when it would be unsafe. Upward white arrow beside a downward red arrow on blue.
Oncoming traffic must give way. Upward white arrow beside a downward red arrow on blue.
Knowledge check. Does seeing a warning sign tell you an exact safe speed?
Remember: Identify the instruction and turn it into an early action. The illustrated sign reference is prepared separately from this text.
Your goal: Interpret signs, panels, markings and signals together, including authorised directions.

Requirements. Follow the traffic instructions that apply to you. Where an instruction differs from a general traffic rule, the instruction governs. A steady traffic-light indication takes precedence over a yield or stop sign; a police officer's direction takes precedence over the rules and ordinary traffic instructions. This is not a rule that a green signal cancels every other restriction. Authorised guards also give traffic directions that must be followed. Traffic Regulation, chapter 2 §§2–4
Authorised directions Separate examples. A static picture does not show the complete movement; read the description and the official instruction.

Traffic approaching the officer from the front or rear must stop; traffic approaching from the sides may proceed. The officer's continuing orientation matters even after the arm movement. Officer faces the viewer with one arm extended sideways.
Police stop instruction — front and rear. Officer faces the viewer with one arm extended sideways.
Continue the learning
Stop if the officer's palm faces you. A stop paddle may be used instead. Officer raises a palm towards approaching traffic.
Police stop instruction — palm facing you. Officer raises a palm towards approaching traffic.
Stop if the guard faces you. A red lamp is used in darkness; an authorised stop sign marked Vakt may also be used. Guard faces approaching traffic and holds a red flag sideways.
Traffic guard — stop. Guard faces approaching traffic and holds a red flag sideways.
The guard identifier must be worn on the front and back. It identifies the role rather than giving a separate movement instruction. Garment identification panel bearing VAKT.
Traffic guard identifier. Garment identification panel bearing VAKT.

For ordinary vehicle signals: red means stop; red and amber together still mean stop, with green approaching. Green permits movement, subject to other duties and space ahead. Amber means stop unless, when green changes to amber, you are already so close that stopping would be dangerous. Flashing amber requires particular caution; read the signs and applicable rules. Arrow signals apply to the direction indicated. Road Signs Regulation, chapter 3 §§3–6

Ordinary vehicle signals Red, red/amber, green and amber appear in that order. Flashing amber is a separate condition, not the next stage of the normal cycle. Arrow indications apply to the direction shown.
Stop before the stop line or, if none, before the signal. An outline arrow limits the indication to the direction shown. Red left arrow, red full lamp and red bicycle signal examples.
Red vehicle signal. Red left arrow, red full lamp and red bicycle signal examples.
Green is about to follow, but the stop instruction still applies. Do not start merely because amber has appeared. Red and amber illuminated together in arrow, full-lamp and bicycle examples.
Red and amber vehicle signal. Red and amber illuminated together in arrow, full-lamp and bicycle examples.

You may proceed subject to the remaining traffic duties. A green arrow applies to its direction, including when another signal indication appears simultaneously. Green arrow, green full lamp and green bicycle signal examples.
Green vehicle signal. Green arrow, green full lamp and green bicycle signal examples.
Continue the learning

Stop, unless the change from green occurs when stopping would be dangerous because you are already too close. An outline arrow limits the indication to its direction. Amber arrow, amber full lamp and amber bicycle signal examples.
Amber vehicle signal. Amber arrow, amber full lamp and amber bicycle signal examples.
Separate condition: flashing amber
Proceed with particular caution and apply the other instructions and traffic rules. Flashing is not demonstrated by the still image. Amber flashing lamp represented by a still drawing.
Flashing amber vehicle signal. Amber flashing lamp represented by a still drawing.

A red lane-control cross closes the lane; a green downward arrow allows its use; a diagonal amber arrow tells you to move in the indicated direction. Make any lane change safely. Signals for pedestrians or public transport are not automatically instructions for your car. Road Signs Regulation, chapter 3 §§7–15
Lane and public-transport signals Lane-control signals and public-transport signals are separate sets. Follow the instruction that applies to your lane and traffic. Lane control
The lane and, where applicable, its adjacent shoulder must not be used for traffic. Red cross on black.
Lane-control red cross. Red cross on black.
Change lane in an indicated direction, making the manoeuvre safely. Amber arrows point diagonally down to both sides in one example and down-right in another.
Lane-control amber arrow. Amber arrows point diagonally down to both sides in one example and down-right in another.
The lane may be used. Other traffic restrictions and safety duties still apply. Green arrow points down.
Lane-control green arrow. Green arrow points down.
Public transport
Stop before the line or, without one, before the signal. This is a signal for the traffic it controls, not a general car signal. White S in the upper lamp of a public-transport signal.
Public-transport signal — S. White S in the upper lamp of a public-transport signal.
A proceed indication is about to follow, but the stop instruction remains in force. White S and horizontal bar lit together.
Public-transport signal — S and horizontal bar. White S and horizontal bar lit together.
The controlled vehicle or tram may proceed. An arrow applies to its indicated direction. White vertical bar in the lower signal lamp.
Public-transport signal — vertical bar or arrow. White vertical bar in the lower signal lamp.
Continue the learning
Stop unless the change from the vertical indication occurs so late that stopping would be dangerous. This is not the proceed indication. White horizontal bar in the middle signal lamp.
Public-transport signal — horizontal bar. White horizontal bar in the middle signal lamp.

Markings. A broken centre or lane line identifies a boundary; it does not promise that overtaking is safe. A warning line indicates that crossing is unsuitable because of conditions and may precede a continuous line. Continuous lines and hatched areas have crossing restrictions, with specified exceptions such as a necessary passage around an obstruction under particular caution. A painted line is not an invitation to improvise an exception. Road Signs Regulation, chapter 4, M1/M3/M8/M9 · Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§9–11
Read the marking on your side For paired lines, identify the line immediately beside your side of the road. The line on the far side does not grant you permission to cross.

A broken line separates opposing directions or adjacent lanes, depending on its position. It does not guarantee that crossing or overtaking is safe. Two examples of a broken white line on a dark road background.
Centre or lane line. Two examples of a broken white line on a dark road background.
Continue the learning
Crossing this line is unsuitable because of the traffic conditions. It may also warn of a continuous line ahead. Long white strokes with short gaps.
Warning line. Long white strokes with short gaps.
Crossing restrictions apply according to the type of continuous line and the traffic rules. Do not invent an exception merely because the road appears clear. Single and double continuous white lines.
Continuous line. Single and double continuous white lines.
Vehicles must not normally enter the marked area. Only the specified traffic-rule exceptions can justify crossing it. White hatched area on a dark road background.
Hatched area. White hatched area on a dark road background.
The continuous line governs a driver on its side of the marking. Do not treat the broken line on the other side as permission to change lanes. Broken white line beside a continuous line.
Broken line beside a continuous line. Broken white line beside a continuous line.
Continue the learning
The continuous-line side restricts lane changes; the warning-line side indicates that crossing is unsuitable. Warning line beside a continuous line.
Warning line beside a continuous line. Warning line beside a continuous line.
A driver on the warning-line side should recognise that crossing is unsuitable because of the conditions. Broken centre line beside a warning line.
Centre line beside a warning line. Broken centre line beside a warning line.

Supplementary panels qualify the sign above them: read the distance, length, direction, time or vehicle symbol as part of the instruction. A distance to a hazard and the length of a hazardous stretch answer different questions. Supplementary panels
Read the supplementary panel Independent recognition examples. A supplementary panel qualifies the sign above it on the road; these examples are not stacked into an invented instruction.
The panel identifies the beginning and end of the affected section. Distinguish this from a distance to a single feature.
Two official outline distance-range examples: 200–800 m and 0–1,2 km.
Continue the learning
This states how far ahead the main sign's subject lies, rather than the length of the affected section.
Official outline distance panel reading 100 m.
Used below B1, this provides advance notice of a stop requirement at the indicated distance. It is not an instruction to stop at this advance sign. STOPP 200 m: a stop requirement 200 metres ahead.
Distance to a stop requirement. STOPP 200 m: a stop requirement 200 metres ahead.
Continue the learning

Unbracketed black/white times apply on weekdays other than the day before a Sunday or public holiday; brackets mean those preceding days; red means Sundays and public holidays. A named day governs regardless of its category. A period crossing midnight continues into the next day.
Official time-panel example: outline 8–17, bracketed outline (8–14), and red 8–13.
The sign above applies only to the vehicle or road-user group shown on the panel. Read time qualifications as part of the same instruction.
Official outline supplementary panel containing a heavy goods vehicle symbol.
Continue the learning
Two-ended arrows indicate both sides of the sign; a downward arrow marks the end; a left or right arrow indicates that direction. Read the exact form and context. Black arrows point left and right.
Extent of the instruction. Black arrows point left and right.

Two-ended arrows indicate both sides of the sign; a downward arrow marks the end; a left or right arrow indicates that direction. Read the exact form and context. Black arrow points down, marking the end of the instruction.
Extent of the instruction. Black arrow points down, marking the end of the instruction.
Follow the indicated direction to the feature identified by the main sign. A right-turn arrow on blue.
Direction to the signed feature. A right-turn arrow on blue.
Continue the learning
Read the text as a qualification of the sign above; it supplies information not expressed by the other panels.
Official outline supplementary panel with the word Text.
This symbol identifies passenger cars in the surrounding sign or panel.
Official outline reference showing a passenger car.
Continue the learning
This identifies a passenger car towing a släpkärra. Do not use it as a universal illustration of every trailer classification.
Official outline reference showing the rear of a passenger car with an attached small trailer.
This symbol identifies bicycles and class II mopeds, not class I mopeds.
Official outline reference showing a bicycle, representing cycles and class II mopeds.
Continue the learning
The sign above applies only to the vehicle or road-user group shown on the panel. Read time qualifications as part of the same instruction. Passenger car.
Vehicle or road-user qualification. Passenger car.
The sign above applies only to the vehicle or road-user group shown on the panel. Read time qualifications as part of the same instruction. Passenger car with centre-axle trailer.
Vehicle or road-user qualification. Passenger car with centre-axle trailer.
The sign above applies only to the vehicle or road-user group shown on the panel. Read time qualifications as part of the same instruction. Bicycle and class II moped.
Vehicle or road-user qualification. Bicycle and class II moped.
Apply the learning
A green signal and a queue beyond the junction. Opposing traffic is separated and the stop line is before the crossing road. The scene is illustrative, not to scale.

Worked decision. Your signal is green, but a queue fills the space beyond the junction. Wait where you will not obstruct crossing traffic rather than entering a space you cannot clear. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §20
Knowledge check. Does amber mean accelerate to beat red?
Remember: Read the whole instruction and the space beyond it.
Your goal: Use direction, facility and service signs to prepare route choices early.

Direction information appears before and at decision points. An advance direction sign helps you understand a junction or exit before reaching it; lane direction information helps you select a suitable lane. Direction signs for walking and cycling serve those modes and should not be mistaken for a car route. Facility, service and tourism signs help locate destinations; they do not cancel restrictions on access. Road Signs Regulation, chapter 2, F/G/H/I families
Advance directions and lane choice Sample destinations are independent examples. They do not describe one continuous route.
Use this advance junction or roundabout diagram to plan your route before the decision point. Advance diagram: route 50 towards Falun ahead; Lindesberg to the right.
Advance direction diagram. Advance diagram: route 50 towards Falun ahead; Lindesberg to the right.
This is an alternative advance-direction layout. Read the destinations and the junction diagram before choosing your route. Roundabout advance diagram: Örebro ahead, Kumla left and Katrineholm right.
Advance direction diagram — alternative. Roundabout advance diagram: Örebro ahead, Kumla left and Katrineholm right.
Continue the learning
Read the listed directions and approach distance before the junction or roundabout. Destination table: route 80 ahead; route 272 towards Bollnäs left; Forsbacka right; junction 500 m ahead.
Advance destination table. Destination table: route 80 ahead; route 272 towards Bollnäs left; Forsbacka right; junction 500 m ahead.
An exit is ahead at the indicated distance. Prepare the appropriate lane safely. Advance exit towards Ornäs, 500 m ahead, while route 50 continues ahead.
Advance exit information. Advance exit towards Ornäs, 500 m ahead, while route 50 continues ahead.
The sign points to a destination at a junction. Any stated distance is in whole kilometres. Right-pointing sign to Nyköping, 23 km.
Direction sign. Right-pointing sign to Nyköping, 23 km.
This lists directions near a junction or roundabout, including at an exit from a roundabout. Destination table: Gävle via route 80 ahead, Bollnäs via route 272 left, Forsbacka right.
Destination table. Destination table: Gävle via route 80 ahead, Bollnäs via route 272 left, Forsbacka right.
Continue the learning
The exit begins at this sign. Do not make a late unsafe lane change to reach it. Exit sign pointing towards Mora via route 70 and towards Enköping.
Exit direction sign. Exit sign pointing towards Mora via route 70 and towards Enköping.
Use the lane or lanes beneath the relevant destination. Read any distance given for an upcoming exit. Overhead destinations: Boda on the left panel; Falun via route 50 on the right panel.
Overhead lane destinations. Overhead destinations: Boda on the left panel; Falun via route 50 on the right panel.
Choose a suitable lane for the direction you intend to take at the junction. Lane diagram before a junction, including left, ahead and right movements.
Lane choices before a junction. Lane diagram before a junction, including left, ahead and right movements.
This identifies the interchange number and may include an exit designation. Interchange number 75.
Interchange number. Interchange number 75.
Walking and cycling routes These walking and cycling examples are separate from car-route guidance. Standalone symbols retain their own official meaning.
Read the road-user symbol and destination. A route for walking or cycling is not automatically a car route. Bicycle direction to Centrum, pointing right.
Walking or cycling direction sign. Bicycle direction to Centrum, pointing right.
Directions and kilometre distances are given for the indicated road-user group. Bicycle destinations: Kumla 5 km ahead; Haga 0.2 km left.
Walking or cycling destination table. Bicycle destinations: Kumla 5 km ahead; Haga 0.2 km left.
This identifies a place for orientation along the route. Place name Lundby on a walking/cycling route sign.
Place name on a walking or cycling route. Place name Lundby on a walking/cycling route sign.
Read the distances in kilometres together with the road-user symbol. Bicycle destination Centrum, 3 km.
Walking or cycling distance board. Bicycle destination Centrum, 3 km.
Continue the learning
This identifies a specially designated cycle route; the colour scheme can vary. Bicycle pictogram identifying a cycle route.
Cycle route. Bicycle pictogram identifying a cycle route.
This symbol identifies bicycles and class II mopeds, not class I mopeds.
Official outline reference showing a bicycle, representing cycles and class II mopeds.
Continue the learning
This identifies pedestrians as the group covered by the surrounding instruction.
Official outline reference showing an adult and child walking.

Learning approach. Know your next destination or route number, look for advance information and compare it with the road layout. Check the lane and movement required, then establish a safe opportunity to position the car. This is easier when navigation is prepared while parked and passengers understand that late instructions may be declined.

A symbol or route number may be easier to recognise than a place name. Learn the relevant symbols from the official catalogue rather than inventing an interpretation. Information signs can describe a changed route or other conditions; read enough of the message early to decide safely. Transportstyrelsen: sign catalogue
Destinations and route numbers Compare route numbers and solid or dashed borders. The permanent alternative-route example is distinct from temporary orange guidance.
The destinations inside the bracket share the route shown below its point. Pajala and Övertorneå grouped above the shared route via Kiruna.
Grouped destinations. Pajala and Övertorneå grouped above the shared route via Kiruna.
This identifies a place for orientation. It is not by itself a speed-limit sign. Place name Nyköping.
Place name. Place name Nyköping.
This identifies the name of a road or route. Road name Hemvägen.
Road name. Road name Hemvägen.
Distances to the listed destinations are shown in whole kilometres. Distances: Stockholm 105 km; Södertälje 71 km.
Distance board. Distances: Stockholm 105 km; Södertälje 71 km.
Continue the learning
This identifies a numbered route. A dashed border means the road leads towards the numbered route rather than necessarily being that route itself. E4 route shield with solid border.
Road number. E4 route shield with solid border.

This identifies a numbered route. A dashed border means the road leads towards the numbered route rather than necessarily being that route itself. E4 route shield with dashed border, indicating a route towards E4.
Road number. E4 route shield with dashed border, indicating a route towards E4.
This identifies a numbered route. A dashed border means the road leads towards the numbered route rather than necessarily being that route itself. Route 58 shield with solid border.
Road number. Route 58 shield with solid border.

This identifies a numbered route. A dashed border means the road leads towards the numbered route rather than necessarily being that route itself. Route 58 shield with dashed border, indicating a route towards route 58.
Road number. Route 58 shield with dashed border, indicating a route towards route 58.
Continue the learning
This marks a permanent alternative route for the numbered road. Distinguish it from temporary orange diversion guidance. Permanent alternative route for road 58.
Permanent diversion route. Permanent alternative route for road 58.
Read the actual message: it supplies important information for safety or passage that is not given another way. Message: Vägsaltning upphör — road salting ends.
Traffic information. Message: Vägsaltning upphör — road salting ends.

Requirement. Destination signs can permit using the lane suited to your onward route, but changing into it still has to be safe. Do not cross a continuous lane boundary merely because you have chosen the wrong exit. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§7, 9 and 43
Apply the learning
Drivers approach a decision point in marked lanes. Plan the permitted route early. The illustration does not assign destinations to particular lanes.
Continue on the permitted route after a missed turn and find another safe opportunity. Not to scale.

Worked decision. A navigation instruction arrives after a driver has passed the safe lane-change opportunity. The driver continues in the permitted direction and finds another route. A missed turn is a planning problem; a sudden crossing of lanes creates a traffic problem.
Knowledge check. A service sign shows fuel at a junction. Does that guarantee that every approach or vehicle may enter the access road?
Facilities and services Separate reference examples for recognising facilities, services and tourist routes.
This identifies a fuel facility. It does not cancel access restrictions on the approach road. Fuel pump.
Fuel. Fuel pump.
This identifies a facility for externally charging an electrically powered vehicle. Car connected to a charging unit.
Vehicle charging station. Car connected to a charging unit.
This points to a hospital with an emergency department, not simply any medical facility. Red cross on white within a blue sign.
Hospital with an emergency department. Red cross on white within a blue sign.
Continue the learning
Information is available at the indicated place. Nearby text may identify the type of information. Lower-case information letter i.
Information point. Lower-case information letter i.
This identifies a rest area with a toilet accessible to people with mobility impairments. Picnic table and tree.
Rest area. Picnic table and tree.
The road or route has tourist interest. Ordinary traffic restrictions still apply. White flower on brown.
Tourist route. White flower on brown.
Remember: A route can be corrected later. An unsafe last-second manoeuvre cannot be planned away afterwards.
Your goal: Explain how observation, speed, reaction, braking, grip and following space affect your options.

Requirements. Choose a speed that preserves control and lets you stop within the road you can see and before a foreseeable obstruction. Your distance from the vehicle ahead must allow for it slowing or stopping. Weather, visibility, road condition, vehicle condition and loading all matter. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §§2 and 14–16

For an ordinary car, the general speed limits are 50 km/h within a built-up area and 70 km/h outside it, unless another applicable limit has been prescribed. The motorway default is 110 km/h; 120 km/h can be prescribed. Local and road-specific limits often differ, and a lower vehicle-combination limit still applies. Read the current signs and conditions rather than selecting a speed from the road’s appearance. Traffic Regulation, chapter 3 §17, chapter 4 §20 and chapter 9 §1
Limits and road regimes Numeric maximum-speed examples are independent. Start and end types are labelled individually; unequal values do not form a sequence.
Do not exceed the displayed speed in km/h. A junction alone does not necessarily end the limit, and conditions may require a lower speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 30: maximum 30 km/h.
Maximum speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 30: maximum 30 km/h.
Continue the learning
Do not exceed the displayed speed in km/h. A junction alone does not necessarily end the limit, and conditions may require a lower speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 40: maximum 40 km/h.
Maximum speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 40: maximum 40 km/h.
Do not exceed the displayed speed in km/h. A junction alone does not necessarily end the limit, and conditions may require a lower speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 50: maximum 50 km/h.
Maximum speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 50: maximum 50 km/h.
Do not exceed the displayed speed in km/h. A junction alone does not necessarily end the limit, and conditions may require a lower speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 70: maximum 70 km/h.
Maximum speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 70: maximum 70 km/h.
Continue the learning
Do not exceed the displayed speed in km/h. A junction alone does not necessarily end the limit, and conditions may require a lower speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 80: maximum 80 km/h.
Maximum speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 80: maximum 80 km/h.
Do not exceed the displayed speed in km/h. A junction alone does not necessarily end the limit, and conditions may require a lower speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 110: maximum 110 km/h.
Maximum speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 110: maximum 110 km/h.
Do not exceed the displayed speed in km/h. A junction alone does not necessarily end the limit, and conditions may require a lower speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 120: maximum 120 km/h.
Maximum speed. Red-bordered yellow circle displaying 120: maximum 120 km/h.
Continue the learning
The temporary signed speed limit ends. Establish the speed limit that now applies rather than assuming there is none. 30 crossed by diagonal black lines: temporary 30 km/h limit ends.
End of temporary speed limit. 30 crossed by diagonal black lines: temporary 30 km/h limit ends.
A built-up area begins. Establish the applicable speed limit and other rules; a separate sign may prescribe a different limit. Black settlement skyline on white.
Built-up area. Black settlement skyline on white.
The built-up area ends. Check the rules and signed limits for the road ahead. Settlement skyline crossed by a red diagonal.
End of built-up area. Settlement skyline crossed by a red diagonal.
The sign recommends a lower speed because of the road's conditions or measures. Distinguish it from a C31 legal maximum. Blue sign reading max 30 km/tim: recommended 30 km/h.
Recommended lower speed. Blue sign reading max 30 km/tim: recommended 30 km/h.
Continue the learning
The signed recommendation ends. Continue to choose a speed suited to conditions and legal limits. Blue max 30 km/tim sign crossed by a red diagonal.
End of recommended lower speed. Blue max 30 km/tim sign crossed by a red diagonal.

This variable sign recommends a temporary lower maximum because of current conditions. The recommendation is below the legal maximum. White 50 on a dark variable-sign background: recommended maximum 50 km/h.
Recommended maximum speed. White 50 on a dark variable-sign background: recommended maximum 50 km/h.
The temporary speed recommendation ends. White diagonal lines on a dark background.
End of recommended maximum speed. White diagonal lines on a dark background.

Think of stopping in two parts. During the time between noticing a hazard and beginning effective braking, the vehicle still travels. After that, it travels while slowing. More speed consumes more distance during the same delay and increases the energy that must be removed. Less available friction reduces what the tyres can do for braking and steering. Trafikverket: speed and impact · VTI friction report, sections 4.2–4.3
Continue the learning

Illustrative calculation, not a stopping-distance prediction. A speed of 50 km/h is approximately 13.9 metres per second: 50 ÷ 3.6. If a hypothetical response delay is one second, that is about 14 metres before braking begins. At 80 km/h the same assumed delay consumes about 22 metres. These figures are unit conversions using an assumed delay; people do not all react in one second, and braking distance has not yet been added.

Learning approach. Scan far enough ahead to see developing situations, while revisiting the near area, mirrors and places where someone may enter. Avoid staring at one hazard until everything else disappears from attention. Increase your margin when information is poor. A timed following-gap check can help you notice a short gap, but no fixed number is safe in every condition.

Safety advice · Check a timed gap. For the three-second following-distance guideline, select a fixed roadside point, such as a pole or sign. When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, start counting at a steady seconds pace. Stop when the front of your car reaches the same point. Arriving before three seconds indicates a short gap against that guideline: ease back smoothly and check again. Three seconds is a guideline, not a statutory fixed interval or a guarantee; poor grip, visibility or other hazards require more space and an appropriate speed. Keep observing the road while counting. NSW Government: fixed-point following-gap method

Fixed-point example. The car ahead passes a sign. You count “one thousand and one, one thousand and two, one thousand and three”. If your car reaches the sign while you are still on “two”, increase the gap smoothly. At a hypothetical constant 60 km/h, three seconds represents 60 ÷ 3.6 × 3 = 50 metres. A timed gap therefore represents more metres at higher speed, without requiring you to estimate metres by eye.
Margins and braking distance

Safety advice · When someone follows too closely. Increase your gap to the vehicle ahead gradually, allowing you to ease off and brake more gently if traffic slows. This gives the following driver more time to respond. Do not brake sharply to warn or punish them, or accelerate into an unsafe speed. If an emergency requires braking, brake as necessary; this advice does not mean withholding it. Northern Ireland government: tailgater response

Tailgater example. Maya has a close follower and sees brake lights farther ahead. She eases off early to create room in front and slows progressively. She cannot control the follower, but she can reduce the need for a sudden stop.

Physical explanation · Twice the speed. With the same effective grip and braking deceleration on the same gradient, braking distance is approximately proportional to speed squared: 2 × speed → 4 × braking distance. In a constant-deceleration model, distance = speed² ÷ (2 × deceleration), with speed in metres per second. Doubling speed multiplies the numerator by four. Real conditions and brake response can change; this is a comparison under stated assumptions. Trafikverket: VGU braking-distance equation

Hypothetical comparison. Assume a level road, unchanged vehicle/load/grip, constant braking deceleration of 5 m/s² and a one-second response delay. At 40 km/h, braking distance is about 12.3 m and reaction distance 11.1 m. At 80 km/h they are 49.4 m and 22.2 m: braking quadruples while reaction distance doubles. Total stopping distances are about 23.5 m and 71.6 m, so the total does not quadruple. These invented model conditions explain the relationship; they are not predicted stopping distances for your car.
A rough calculation method

Approximate exercise model · Keep the methods separate. Define v as speed in km/h and t as the supplied reaction time in seconds. Exact constant-speed reaction distance is (v ÷ 3.6) × t metres; braking is not included. When an exercise specifies the rough method below, use both rough estimates together rather than substituting an exact reaction value.

Rough reaction estimate: R = (v ÷ 10) × t × 3 metres. Divide speed by ten, multiply by the supplied seconds, then by three. Trafiko: approximate stopping method documents the one-second shortcut; multiplication by a supplied t is editorial proportional arithmetic. Half a second gives half the one-second estimate; two seconds gives twice it. These are supplied exercise inputs, not claims about every driver's reaction time.

Rough braking estimate: B = (v ÷ 10)² × 0.4 metres. Divide speed by ten, square that result, then multiply by 0.4. Trafiko: approximate stopping method describes this shortcut under good-brake, good-tyre and dry-asphalt assumptions. The coefficient is an exercise assumption, not a universal result for a real car or road. Supplied reaction time does not change the braking part in this model.

Rough total: S = R + B. Calculate both parts separately with metres, then add. Keep decimal precision during the working; round only the final result if a precision is requested. These shortcuts teach arithmetic, not a safe-distance guarantee or a prediction for an actual hazard.

Source and assumption limits. Trafiko is a commercial teaching source, cited only for these approximate shortcuts. Trafikverket: stopping-distance principles supports reaction plus braking and dependence on speed and conditions, but does not supply these constants. Its illustrated distances have different assumptions and must not be mixed with this model. Real stopping depends on grip, gradient, tyres, brakes, response and other conditions. Retain the exact conversion and separate constant-deceleration comparison above under their own assumptions.
Apply the rough model
Worked approximate examples · Calculate both parts. Use the rough exercise equations consistently; each reaction time below is a supplied hypothetical input.
Example A · 40 km/h and 0.5 seconds. First v ÷ 10 = 4. Reaction R = 4 × 0.5 × 3 = 6 m. Braking B = 4² × 0.4 = 6.4 m. Total S = 6 + 6.4 = 12.4 m. The half-second input affects reaction, not braking.

Example B · 70 km/h and one second. First v ÷ 10 = 7. Reaction R = 7 × 1 × 3 = 21 m. Braking B = 7² × 0.4 = 19.6 m. Total S = 21 + 19.6 = 40.6 m. Squaring seven gives 49; do not multiply speed itself by 0.4.

Example C · 50 km/h and two seconds. First v ÷ 10 = 5. Reaction R = 5 × 2 × 3 = 30 m. Braking B = 5² × 0.4 = 10 m. Total S = 30 + 10 = 40 m. Doubling reaction time doubles this model's reaction estimate, leaving braking unchanged.

Compare separately with exact conversion. At 50 km/h and two seconds, exact constant-speed reaction distance is (50 ÷ 3.6) × 2 = about 27.8 m, compared with the shortcut's 30 m. Dividing the shortcut factor 0.3 by the exact conversion factor 1 ÷ 3.6 gives 1.08: an 8% overestimate for reaction distance. Mixing 27.8 m with rough braking of 10 m gives about 37.8 m, not the exercise model's 40 m. Keep exact conversion separate from the rough-model answer.

Try the approximate process. Calculate reaction, braking and total for (A) 30 km/h and 0.5 seconds, (B) 80 km/h and one second, and (C) 100 km/h and two seconds. Give each part in metres, check the square, then add. Answers are in the separate lesson answer section.
Apply the learning
A driver approaches a queue on a divided road. The illustrated gap is not a measured safe following distance. Look ahead and leave room to respond.

Worked decision. You can see over the roof of the car ahead that traffic is slowing. Ease your approach early rather than waiting for its brake lights at a short distance. The benefit is having choices before braking becomes urgent.

Knowledge check. (1) If response delay doubles at the same speed, what happens to reaction distance? (2) How do you time a three-second following gap? (3) Why increase the forward gap when someone follows too closely? (4) With unchanged braking deceleration, how does doubled speed affect braking distance, and does total stopping distance also quadruple? (5) Complete the three approximate exercises above and explain why you should keep exact reaction conversion separate.
